<file path="docs/deliveries/components/timeline.md">
# Timeline

One shared component for ordered steps, recorded events, and activity feeds.
Import `Timeline` and `TimelineItem` from `@blume/sidecar-ui`.

## Choose a presentation

| Variant    | Marker                                      | Use for                                    |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| `steps`    | Small bordered circle with a number or icon | Setup guidance and recorded test steps     |
| `events`   | Quiet dot                                   | Dense phase history with expandable detail |
| `activity` | Unframed custom icon or avatar              | Agent and tool activity                    |

Use `comfortable` density when rows contain explanations or screenshots.
Use `compact` for short event summaries, and `dense` for one-line rows packed close in a
narrow column (the delivery page column's timeline); there a `steps` marker is a 16px circle with
a small bold number. All variants share the rail, alignment,
typography, focus treatment, and motion. The component preserves the order supplied
by its caller; it does not reorder history or infer completion.

## Compose a timeline

```tsx
<Timeline variant="steps" density="comfortable" aria-label="Recorded test steps">
  <TimelineItem marker={1} title="Restore the basket" tone="success">
    <p>The saved basket is visible after restarting.</p>
    <EvidenceGallery />
  </TimelineItem>
</Timeline>
```

Keep a visible status label when color carries status. Marker numbers are decorative;
the ordered list conveys sequence. Give the timeline an accessible name.

### Recorded steps

Numbers, status colors, and evidence share one aligned rail.

![Shared numbered timeline with test evidence](../../../design-assets/ui-principles/timeline-shared-steps.png)

### Expandable history

A compact event header opens detail beneath the same content alignment.

![Shared event timeline with an expanded phase row](../../../design-assets/ui-principles/timeline-shared-events.png)

## Props

### Timeline

| Prop                              | Values / purpose                                             |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `variant`                         | `steps` (default), `events`, `activity`                      |
| `density`                         | `comfortable` (default), `compact`, `dense`                  |
| `continueBefore`, `continueAfter` | Join adjacent history groups when older entries are revealed |
| Standard list attributes          | Accessible name, ID, and placement classes                   |

### TimelineItem

| Prop                           | Purpose                                                                 |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `title`, `metadata`            | Primary row label and supporting information                            |
| `marker`                       | Number, icon, or avatar; ignored visually by the dot variant            |
| `tone`                         | `neutral`, `accent`, `success`, `danger`, `warning`, `info`, `phase`    |
| `children`                     | Description, evidence, details, and action buttons                      |
| `collapsible`                  | Native keyboard-accessible disclosure                                   |
| `defaultExpanded`              | Initial state for an uncontrolled disclosure                            |
| `expanded`, `onExpandedChange` | Controlled disclosure state                                             |
| `highlighted`, `emphasized`    | Temporary row highlight or marker emphasis                              |
| `disclosureRef`                | Native details ref, used by graph-driven phase reveal                   |
| `variant`, `density`           | Optional row-level overrides                                            |
| `last`                         | Explicit rail termination for grouped activity feeds                    |
| `as`                           | `li` by default; `div` for existing feeds that own their list semantics |

`phase` tone uses the existing `data-phase` palette through DeliveryVisuals.
Other tones use the shared opaque badge palette. Do not pass arbitrary CSS colors.

## Expansion and actions

```tsx
<Timeline variant="events" aria-label="Phase history">
  <TimelineItem
    title="Build"
    metadata="8 min"
    collapsible
    expanded={expanded}
    onExpandedChange={setExpanded}
  >
    <p>Updated checkout recovery.</p>
    <Button type="button" variant="outline">
      Inspect changes
    </Button>
  </TimelineItem>
</Timeline>
```

Put action buttons in the body, not inside the disclosure summary. Enter and Space
operate the native summary. Closed content leaves the focus order. Opening and
closing use the shared disclosure motion and respect reduced motion.

## Where it is used

| View                              | Composition                                            |
| --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| Empty delivery page               | Numbered setup steps                                   |
| Delivery phase history            | `PhaseTimelineItem` adapter, expandable event rows     |
| Verification and test-run detail  | `EvidenceStepTimeline` adapter, numbered status steps  |
| Agent transcript activity         | `ActivityRow` adapter, activity markers and timestamps |
| Setup, usage, and change previews | `StepTimeline` compatibility adapter                   |
| Legacy phase heading              | Shared item with phase icon and metadata               |

Adapters own domain content. `Timeline` owns every rail, marker frame, spacing,
and disclosure recipe. Existing StepTimeline callers remain compatible while
sharing the new rendering; known legacy semantic color tokens map to timeline tones.

Storybook: **Components → Timeline** includes steps, expandable history, controlled
expansion, and activity examples. The history story checks keyboard disclosure.
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/agent-messaging.md">
# Agent messaging

Any agent with the Blume plugin installed can message any other agent on the same
Blume account, across harnesses. The person using Blume can message any agent as well.
Blume stores and routes every message. Each harness delivers messages through the plugin
components that work best in that harness. See [what "the plugin" means](plugin-architecture-levers.md#what-the-plugin-means).

Decisions (Olav, 2026-09-28):

- The standalone Inbox tab is removed. Messaging lives on each agent: open an agent from a
  delivery's or a project's Agents tab to see its message history and a composer. The old
  `/inbox` route redirects to Projects.
- Scope is the whole account. Agents can find and message every non-revoked agent
  on the account, and the list shows each agent's project.
- A message can stand alone. Linking it to a delivery is optional, and a linked
  message also appears on that delivery.
- The installer writes the hooks file (`hooks/hooks.json`, with an absolute script path)
  into the plugin in both harnesses. In Codex it then marks Blume's hooks, and only
  Blume's, trusted using Codex's own `hooks/list` and `config/batchWrite`, the same calls
  as Codex's `/hooks` screen.
- Delivery comes in tiers (Olav, 2026-09-28). Tier 1 works the same way in every
  harness: new messages come back with the agent's next Blume tool result. Tier 2 adds
  one hook script shared by Claude Code and Codex, which delivers between any tool calls
  and before a turn ends. Both tiers deliver only while a session is running. Waking an
  idle session is a later, optional tier: Claude Code's `asyncRewake`, and Codex's queue
  (`thread/queue/add` via `codex queue`) with a fallback to the next turn.

## Identity

An agent is a harness **session**, not a plugin installation or a bridge process.

| Harness | Identity | Where the plugin reads it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Code | session id | `CLAUDE_CODE_SESSION_ID` in the MCP server's environment; `session_id` in hook input |
| Codex | root thread id | `_meta.threadId` on each MCP `tools/call`; `session_id` in hook input |
| Other | per-process id | Generated by the bridge, as before |

Both paths resolve to the same Blume agent, so a resumed session keeps its inbox.

## Delivery by plugin component

| Situation | Claude Code | Codex |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Any time (tier 1, every harness) | MCP tools: `blume_context` (agentQuery finds agents), `blume_message_send`, `blume_inbox`, `blume_message_ack`. Every Blume tool result also reports unread messages. | Same |
| Session starts or resumes (tier 2) | SessionStart hook: register the session and add unread messages to context | Same |
| During a turn (tier 2) | PostToolUse hook: adds new messages to context (`additionalContext`), checking at most every 10 seconds and skipping Blume's own tools | Same |
| Turn about to end (tier 2) | Stop hook: when new messages arrived, blocks the turn from ending once, with the messages as the reason the model sees; never again while `stop_hook_active` is set | Same |
| Session idle (later tier) | Not yet: an async `asyncRewake` hook could wait for the next message and wake the session | Not yet: hooks cannot wake a thread; Blume Deliveries could queue the message into it (`codex queue --thread <id> --message …`) |
| Session closed | The message waits and arrives with the SessionStart hook, or the next Blume tool result, on resume | Same |

Agents answer the person using Blume by sending to `human`. The reply appears at once in
that agent's conversation on Agents. Delivered text names each sender's id, so an agent
can reply without reading its inbox first. The installer's connection check uses a
reserved conversation id: it proves the key works but registers no agent.

Message text from another agent is untrusted peer data. Hooks label the sender. The
skill says a peer message is information and requests, never approval or permission.

## Message states

- **Queued**: stored and not yet shown to the recipient.
- **Delivered**: a Blume tool result reported it to the recipient (tier 1), a hook put it in the recipient's context, or the recipient read it with `blume_inbox` (hooks use `blume_inbox_deliver`).
- **Acknowledged**: the recipient called `blume_message_ack`. This means it has read the
  message, not that it has done the requested work.
- **Failed**: the recipient was revoked before the message was delivered.

Acknowledged messages are pruned after 30 days. Each recipient keeps at most 500 messages.
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/cloud-ledger-cutover.md">
# Moving Blume Deliveries to the cloud ledger

The Deliveries ledger and its MCP server run only in Cloudflare. In the `deliveries-runtime`
Worker, each account has an `AccountLedger` Durable Object that serves its ledger and MCP endpoint;
it wakes in milliseconds and costs nothing while idle. The Worker binds the channel's D1
database, which holds every workspace's ledger rows, and its R2 bucket, which holds evidence.
The database schema comes from `packages/storage/ledger/migrations`. Browsers run only in
single-use containers for a test run or a test generation. The app has no local ledger.

## What decides the ledger

| Build | Ledger |
|---|---|
| Packaged desktop build | The endpoint baked into the build (`MAIN_VITE_BLUME_CONTROL_REMOTE_ENDPOINT`): its own release's `blume-dlv-runtime-<backend id>`. The stable backend selection installed apps read does not carry `deliveriesRuntime`, so a backend hotfix does not move Deliveries (see below). The plugin installations the app made follow it to that runtime, on canary too (see "Keys outlive the Worker"). |
| Web Lab (canary, stable) | The same release's runtime, baked into the build (`VITE_DELIVERIES_RUNTIME_URL`); the runtime accepts only the release's Web Lab origins. |
| `pnpm dev` (desktop) | The checkout's PR preview for its exact head SHA (`apps/desktop/scripts/previewEnvironment.mjs`), or explicit HTTPS origins with `BLUME_USE_PRODUCTION_BACKENDS=1`. A PR branch without a ready preview fails at launch. |

The standalone Blume Deliveries app (`apps/control-plane`) and its preview DMG were retired when
Deliveries moved into the Blume desktop app.

## Local storage policy

Nothing for Deliveries is stored in local SQLite without Olav's approval. On this computer the
app keeps only its account session and GitHub token, both encrypted by the OS, in its user
data directory; Electron keeps its own browser caches there. Conversation
history that Blume parses on this computer (from the desktop app's parsers, when they come to
this app) stays local and is not uploaded.

There is no standalone ledger server. Package tests run the hosted routes in process on an
in-memory SQLite copy of the ledger schema, and Web Lab's fixture runtime keeps its ledger in the
browser.

## Release design (decided October 2026)

- **One release train.** Deliveries joins the coordinated Blume canary and stable releases,
  because the two apps are becoming one. `deliveries-runtime` is `release-coupled` in
  `.github/deploy/services.yaml`; PR Checks validates it on pull requests and `main`.
- **A versioned Worker, per-channel storage.** Each release deploys
  `blume-dlv-runtime-<backend id>` with the job container applications
  `blume-dlv-generation-<backend id>` and `blume-dlv-source-<backend id>`. The Worker binds the
  channel's D1 database (`blume-deliveries-canary`, `blume-deliveries`) and evidence bucket
  (`blume-deliveries-evidence-canary`, `blume-deliveries-evidence`), so ledgers survive every
  release. The release applies the migrations in `packages/storage/ledger/migrations` before it
  deploys the Worker. Migrations stay expand-only.
- **Registry.** Release records carry the `deliveries-runtime` component when Deliveries
  ships. The registry probes it with the rest of the backend set, cleans it up, and leaves it
  out of the stable backend selection installed apps read.
- **Keys outlive the Worker.** A canary or stable runtime binds agent connection tokens and plugin
  installation keys to its channel (`blume-release:canary`, `blume-release:stable`), not to its
  per-release address, which the next canary deletes. When the app's runtime moves within its
  channel, its automatic plugin update points each installation it made at the new runtime and
  keeps the key. Canary does not update plugins on its own, but it still makes this move, and
  only the move: each Claude Code and Codex installation the canary app made (its
  `blume-canary://plugin` app link) for an earlier `*.canary.blume-codes.com` runtime gets the
  new runtime as its endpoint (`.mcp.json` `BLUME_CONTROL_ENDPOINT` and `installation.json`
  `endpoint`), and keeps its key, version, files and icon (`pluginMoveDecision` in
  `packages/app/core/src/features/controlPlane/pluginUpdate.ts`, `setup update --endpoint
  --move-only`). Only a later release moves an installation, by the release order in each
  runtime's backend id (`bd-c-<run>-<attempt>`, `bd-s-<version>-<sha>`), never by plugin version,
  so reopening an older canary never moves it back to its deleted runtime; a newer plugin is never
  moved either. Setup moves or automatically updates an installation only while it is still the
  one the app decided on (app link, channel, version, endpoint, key hash), under a lock every
  setup holds, and journals a move so the next pass finishes or undoes a stopped one (and then
  moves it on to its own runtime); a journal whose installation was replaced since is set aside
  without writing (`packages/agent-mcp-node/src/pluginEndpointMove.ts`). E2E and
  partial dev profiles make no move. Installations from a copied command record no app link, so
  no app moves them; they keep the address they were installed with. A PR preview keeps keys
  bound to its own origin.
- **Hotfixes do not move Deliveries.** A backend hotfix deploys the other backends; installed apps
  keep the Deliveries runtime their release baked in, which binds its own release's Auth. Web Lab
  keeps that pair too: while the selection names no Deliveries runtime, it signs in at the Auth
  baked beside its runtime, because the runtime rejects another Auth's tokens
  (`apps/web-lab/src/backendConfig.ts`). Change Deliveries with a release.
- **Expand-only schema.** Every release of a channel reads one database at the same time, so
  migrations after the first only add (`packages/storage/ledger/src/migrationsExpandOnly.test.ts`
  enforces it).
- **Off at launch.** Releases set no Workers AI model (`WEB_TEST_WORKERS_AI_MODEL` is empty), so
  model-led test generation answers that hosted inference is not configured; agents write and
  run their own tests. Auth releases carry no Polar secrets, so checkout answers that billing is
  not configured. Turn either on with its secrets and a canary smoke first.
- **No import.** There are no Deliveries users yet, so existing local ledgers are not imported.

Details are in
[Deliveries in releases](../../../../services/deliveries-runtime/docs/preview.md#deliveries-in-releases).

## Before the first release that carries Deliveries (Olav)

1. Decide job container capacity. Accounts need no container; only test runs (`SourceRuntime`)
   and model-led test generation (`GenerationRuntime`) do, one single-use container per job.
   `max_instances` in `services/deliveries-runtime/wrangler.jsonc` is 3 for each, so at most
   three test runs and three generations run at once across all accounts; a further job cannot
   start until one finishes.
   Set the release numbers before real users arrive.
2. Merge PR #1000.
3. Let canonical Insights Control deploy from main (its workflow runs on the merge), so the
   registry accepts the Deliveries components before a release records them. Releases check this
   first: they stop before any deploy until `https://agents.blume-codes.com/health` reports
   `capabilities.deliveriesRuntime`.
4. Make sure the canary and stable `CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` has Containers and Workers AI access
   besides Workers, and that `CLOUDFLARE_D1_API_TOKEN` can create D1 databases. The release
   runner (`ubuntu-latest`) builds the container images with Docker.
5. Start a canary release (`pnpm release:start -- canary --sha <main sha>` or the admin
   button). It creates the canary database and bucket, applies the ledger migrations, deploys
   the runtime Worker and checks its release identity.
6. After the canary is healthy, promote to stable through the normal stable release.

## Desktop builds

Deliveries is part of the one Blume app, built by the release workflows. A canary or stable build
bakes in its release's Deliveries runtime: the release workflows set
`MAIN_VITE_BLUME_CONTROL_REMOTE_ENDPOINT` to that release's `blume-dlv-runtime-<backend id>`
origin, beside the release's own Auth, and Web Lab gets the same origin as
`VITE_DELIVERIES_RUNTIME_URL`.

## Development plugin installs

Development installs that point at the old local ledger (`127.0.0.1:6211`) stop working. Before
the production release, remove them from `~/.claude` and `~/.codex`
(`node ~/.claude/blume-deliveries/blume-setup.mjs uninstall --harness claude`,
`node ~/.codex/blume-deliveries/blume-setup.mjs uninstall --harness codex`), delete the three
leftover `hooks.state."blume-deliveries@blume:hooks/hooks.json:*"` entries in
`~/.codex/config.toml`, and install the plugin again from the app's Plugin page, which now
installs against the hosted runtime.
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/expected-delivery-process.md">
# Expected delivery process

**Status: draft for user review.** This describes intended behavior, not a claim
that it is implemented. Do not use it as the agent's acceptance checklist until
the user explicitly approves it.

## One connected workflow

Scope: Deliveries in the Blume desktop app (`apps/desktop`; the former standalone
`apps/control-plane` shell is retired) and its plugin, MCP and test framework.

The user describes an outcome. Their agent uses the Blume plugin and MCP to
organize and perform the work. The Electron app shows progress, remaining work,
tests, evidence, and decisions. These surfaces must agree about the same data.

## Setup and conversation entry

- **Minimal setup.** Aim for one copyable prompt to the user's agent or one
  terminal command that installs and connects the plugin. Guide the user through
  any necessary sign-in or consent, then verify the connection. Show the actual
  installed/reported version and capabilities. Avoid manual configuration where
  the agent can do it reliably.
- **Decide whether to use Blume in every new conversation.** Support a preference
  to ask, default to using Blume, or follow rules such as repository scope. Explicit
  user instructions take precedence. Verify GitHub integration and add missing
  support for repository association and the delivery/PR workflow.
- **Make the process discoverable.** The agent must receive the relevant Blume
  instructions at conversation entry. Prefer native harness/plugin mechanisms;
  use hooks if needed for reliable context injection. Verify each supported
  harness rather than assuming installation makes instructions visible.
- **Choose the delivery.** Honor an explicit delivery or new-delivery instruction
  in the initial prompt. Otherwise inspect the repository, branch/PR, and existing
  deliveries. Join a clearly matching delivery; when ambiguous, suggest a match
  or ask whether to join or create. Avoid duplicates and silently joining unrelated
  work. Then start or join through MCP and load its current state before working.

## Phase lifecycle

Use Start, Learn, Plan, Build, Test, Review, Ready, Merge, Deploy, and Live.
Repeated visits and returns to earlier phases retain their history.

The phase says where the work really is ([phases follow reality](../../../../docs/plans/phases-follow-reality.md)).
The lifecycle below is the expected path, not a set of gates: an agent's checkpoint
moves the delivery to the phase it names, and a person can choose any phase from
the phase badge in the delivery's header, forward or back. When a move skips a
step the process expects (approval, evidence, remaining work, a failed deploy),
Blume records it on the new visit and shows it; nothing moves a phase back on its
own.

| Phase | Expected behavior |
| --- | --- |
| **Start** | Establish the outcome and delivery association briefly. Move quickly to Learn if research is needed, otherwise directly to Plan. |
| **Learn** | Resolve relevant unknowns and record findings that inform the work. Then enter Plan. |
| **Plan** | Populate the hierarchical task list and acceptance criteria. Define delivery tests where practical; those tests make the acceptance criteria verifiable. |
| **Build** | Implement the work, using Blume tools to keep tasks and statuses current. Add newly discovered work immediately. Alternate with Test as often as useful. |
| **Test** | Run real ad-hoc tests frequently, inspect results, and return to Build for fixes. Preserve attempts and associate evidence with the tested revision and environment. |
| **Review** | Have the full delivery test suite results ready for human review. Cover all relevant acceptance cases, with steps, screenshots, and other appropriate evidence visible in the review screen. Clearly expose failures and gaps. |
| **Ready** | The human has approved merging the current revision. The agent observes that approval and can proceed to Merge. Passing tests alone is not approval. |
| **Merge** | Show this phase while the agent performs the authorized merge; record its result and evidence. |
| **Deploy** | Show deployment progress and the pipeline/link while deployment is running. Add the deployment URL when available. Follow the established release and promotion process. |
| **Live** | Verify the actual released version and environment, with reviewed evidence. Keep deployment failures, recovery, and rollback history visible. |

### Past phase visits must retain their data

The timeline must explain what actually happened in every previous visit, not
just show a phase name and transition time. Capture visit-specific information
as work happens and retain it when the agent changes phase or revision.

- Learn: relevant findings and decisions. Plan: planned scope, task structure,
  acceptance criteria and material changes.
- Build: tasks worked on/completed, actual file changes and commits when present.
- Test: methods used, related tasks, exact runs/attempts, outcomes and available
  screenshots/artifacts from that pass, including failures before repair.
- Review and later phases: evidence considered, human decisions, merge result,
  deployment pipeline and live verification as applicable.

Bind records to the actual visit, revision and task IDs. Repeated Build/Test
visits must keep their own records; later evidence must not overwrite an earlier
pass or be retroactively attributed to it. Missing or inapplicable data must be
stated honestly, never fabricated. But repeated empty placeholders for work that
actually occurred are a recording/integration defect, not acceptable completion.
Test these historical views in Electron after transitions, reload and resumption.

### Exercise fresh deliveries, not only one long-running fixture

A persistent delivery is useful for repair and resume tests, but is not a substitute
for exercising creation through completion. Run a small representative set of fresh
deliveries plus an existing-delivery join/resume case. Track which trials created
real app-visible deliveries, which ran in isolated accounts/environments, and which
were simulations. Explain this distinction in the proof record.

Demonstrate the full applicable lifecycle for a shipping outcome, including real
human decision boundaries and authorized merge/deploy/live verification in a
disposable test target. Do not bypass approvals or merge the Blume app into main.
A local-only trial stopping at Review proves only that limited path. Record any
blocked later stages explicitly, and do not treat many iterations on one fixture
as evidence of complete onboarding or start-to-finish workflow coverage.

### Task list: always exhaustive, always current

The task tree is the complete account of known work required before this delivery
ships. Planning is its starting point, not a frozen specification.

- Use root tasks for larger items and subtasks for their concrete work.
- Include **all known in-scope work**; do not do hidden work outside the list.
- Exclude work that will not be done before this delivery ships. If scope changes,
  record the change and remove/defer that work from this delivery explicitly.
- Update statuses as work starts, finishes, fails, or becomes blocked. A parent
  with completed and unfinished children is in progress.
- Expect frequent additions and revisions after Plan. Research, implementation,
  and testing continually reveal more work; keep the list exhaustive throughout.

### Task structure, ordering, and test attribution

**Required:** Keep tasks in intended execution order as far as dependencies allow.
Order siblings consistently; do not imply a strict sequence for work that can run
in parallel. Group by meaningful outcome or workstream, with concrete, independently
trackable subtasks. Avoid overlapping roots, miscellaneous buckets, and mixing
unrelated work merely because it occurs in the same phase.

**Strong preference:** The initial plan identifies the major root tasks for the
whole delivery. Most applicable phases after Plan should have corresponding work
in the task tree, including verification, review preparation, merge, deployment,
and live verification when those are in scope. This is coverage, not a requirement
for one root per phase or an empty placeholder for every phase. A phase reports
where the delivery is; a task describes work to finish.

Add discovered detail primarily as subtasks under the appropriate existing root.
Create, split, reorder, or reparent roots when genuinely new scope or a clearer
breakdown warrants it. Root stability must never hide work or force a poor grouping.
Explain material plan changes, preserve task identity/history where possible, and
keep parent status consistent with the remaining children. Do not add release
work that is explicitly outside the delivery's outcome.

**Ad-hoc test attribution:** On every run, the agent must try to identify and link
all directly relevant implementation tasks and any task tracking the testing work.
A run can verify several tasks; a task can have several runs. Keep these as explicit
task-ID relationships, visible from both the result and the related tasks, rather
than relying on a similar title. Record the tested revision and the behavior or
acceptance criterion being checked. If no reliable task match exists, state that
the run is unattributed and why; do not invent a relationship.

For example, a test checking that checkboxes are red links to “Make checkboxes
red” and, if present, “Verify checkbox appearance.” Describe the assertion and
include appropriate visual evidence. Create a separate testing task when it is
meaningful planned or newly discovered work; do not require a new task for every
retry or trivial check. Failures should identify affected work and lead to a
reopened task or a linked repair task. A passing run does not automatically finish
an entire task unless it demonstrates all of that task's acceptance criteria.

### Evidence and approval

Acceptance criteria define what success means; delivery tests should demonstrate
that those criteria hold. Ad-hoc testing supports iteration, but does not replace
complete delivery-suite results at Review. Do not weaken assertions just to pass.
Explain legitimate test changes and retain previous failed attempts.

Revision changes must not inherit stale approval or present old evidence as proof
of new work. Agents cannot manufacture human approval. Merge, Deploy, and Live
should retain reviewed evidence appropriate to each step; when a delivery reaches
them without it (or without approval), the visit records what was skipped and the
delivery shows a "Not approved" note instead of moving back. Fixture or simulated
runs must be distinguishable from real execution; missing evidence is not success.
Applications, deliveries, tests, and evidence belong to the authenticated account.

### Natural-language definitions and generated Playwright

The authored test definition describes intent, human-readable steps and expected
outcomes. It must not require Playwright commands, selectors or an action DSL.
The agent explores the actual application, generates executable Playwright source,
and the runtime executes that source to collect results and evidence. A JSON
operation plan interpreted through Playwright is not a substitute for this contract.

Keep Definition, generated Playwright versions, and Runs distinct. Show the actual
executed source with syntax highlighting, current/version history, author/time,
repair reason and triggering run, intent-preservation explanation, source changes,
and run usage. Support re-exploration from the scenario. Bind each version to its
definition and each run to its actual source/revision. Repairs must preserve the
scenario's intent; preserve older versions and evidence during migration.

### Make automation changes understandable in the UI

Every generated-source version must visibly identify its origin: **Generated**,
**Repaired**, or **Re-explored**. Separately show whether it is a candidate, current,
superseded, or discarded version. Creation of a repair does not mean it was
validated, accepted, or that the product now passes.

For a repair, show who made it and when, the failed run that prompted it, what
broke, what the agent changed, and why the change still tests the same intended
behavior. Show the actual source diff and the validation/replay results, with
links to their steps and captures. Distinguish an automation failure (such as a
stale locator) from a product defect and from a blocked environment; retain an
unknown category when diagnosis is uncertain. Never repair away a product defect
by silently weakening the expected outcome.

Keep authored-definition changes separate from automation repairs. If expected
behavior changes, show a definition revision with its reason and invalidate or
re-evaluate dependent automation and approval as appropriate. An agent's claim
that intent was preserved must be labeled as its explanation, not independent
proof; show the evidence needed to assess that claim.

Use the Playwright version list and detail view for the full change story, a
compact generation/repair status while work runs, and a clear link from each run
to the exact source version it used. Review must show which version and validation
results support the proposed approval, including pending or failed repairs.

### Deployment visibility

For GitHub Actions deployments, the Deploy phase card should show the pipeline
as a graph of jobs and their dependencies, with live queued, running, passed,
failed, cancelled, or skipped states. Include job durations and links to the
workflow run and job logs. Match the run to the delivery's commit and target
environment, including retries; do not display an unrelated latest run.

Use workflow job dependencies for the graph and actual run data for status. If
those dependencies cannot be resolved, show a clear job list instead. While the
pipeline is running, its progress is the primary content. Add the deployment URL
when available; workflow success alone does not prove the release is live.

### Decisions to validate through use

- Keep Build and Test separate initially. Observe real ad-hoc testing during
  implementation before deciding whether merging those phases would work better.
- Validate when the agent can confidently infer an existing delivery and when a
  brief suggestion or question is necessary.
- Verify which harnesses need hooks, and what GitHub integration already exists.
  These are investigation items, not claims of implemented support.

## The agent's iteration loop

**Exercise → observe → diagnose → fix → repeat → record.**

- Start from a realistic user outcome and run the journey using the actual plugin,
  MCP, test runtime, and Electron app. Include both a successful path and a
  deliberate failure followed by recovery.
- Inspect what the user can understand and act on, not just tool responses.
  Identify missing information, confusing transitions, stale state, and unnecessary
  manual work. Fix the underlying issue and repeat the affected journey.
- Check reconnects, restarts, cancellation/retry, account isolation, and revision
  changes. Durable results and evidence must survive replacement of ephemeral
  execution infrastructure. Partial failures must not become false success.
- Leave a short record: scenario, exact code/plugin versions, environment,
  observations, evidence, fixes, and remaining gaps. Separate verified behavior
  from assumptions and prerequisites that are still blocked.

## Challenge the plugin architecture

Use the [architecture levers inventory](plugin-architecture-levers.md) to identify
the available pieces and verify harness support before composing experiments.

**Assume the current tool set and plugin configuration are unlikely to be the
right final design.** They are a baseline to test, not constraints to defend.
Repeated instruction patches are not enough if the tools or interaction model
encourage the wrong behavior. The reviewer should challenge these choices often.

- Draw state and flow diagrams for materially different architectures: how a
  conversation discovers Blume, chooses a delivery, plans, updates work, tests,
  submits evidence, handles human decisions, and resumes after interruption.
  Show which transitions the model chooses and which the system enforces.
- Compare genuinely different tool sets and plugin configurations, not only
  wording changes. Candidates might use many granular tools, a few workflow
  operations, or a state-aware interface that offers the next valid actions.
  Compare native instruction discovery and hooks where relevant.
- Reuse the existing isolated Codex installation as one test environment. Create
  additional separate installations when useful to test alternatives in parallel,
  with independent configuration, plugin versions, project data, and sessions.
  Do not modify the user's normal Codex installation or let variants contaminate
  one another's state.
- Run the same representative outcomes and failure/recovery scenarios against
  each candidate. Keep model, starting state, permissions, and scenario comparable;
  record differences and repeat trials to distinguish reliable behavior from luck.
  Include fresh conversations and resumed/joined deliveries.
- Compare actual agent actions with this document: correct delivery selection,
  exhaustive ordered tasks, phase changes that follow where the work is, task-linked
  tests, revision-correct immutable evidence, and respected human approval (asked
  for and waited on; any skip recorded and told to the person). Also compare
  setup effort, unnecessary questions, tool errors, recovery, latency, and cost.
- Maintain a concise comparison table with transcripts/evidence, failures,
  tradeoffs, and a justified choice. Do not declare a winner from unit tests or
  one successful run. List requirements no candidate has demonstrated yet.

The reviewer should repeatedly ask: **Is this an instruction failure, a tool/API
problem, or a missing system constraint? What alternative architecture was tried?
What evidence shows the chosen design makes the expected behavior reliable?**
Architecture experiments must preserve account isolation and human approval (only a
person approves; Blume records any phase reached without it); changing a tool set is
not permission to bypass those requirements.

### Test with realistic user prompts

Early scripted exercises may test tool contracts and isolated failure handling,
but they do not demonstrate that the plugin supplies the context an agent needs.
Once major mechanical issues are resolved, the primary evaluation must use prompts
similar to what a real user would type. Begin those trials early enough to expose
missing discovery and guidance, rather than saving them for a final demonstration.

For example: “Add a way to save my habits so they are still there when I reopen
the app.” A follow-up might be “It loses them when I restart. Can you fix that?”
An explicit request such as “Continue the checkout delivery” is also realistic.
The user provides the desired outcome, relevant constraints, and genuine decisions.
The plugin, tools, and persisted context must supply the Blume-specific process.

Do not put phase sequences, tool names, task/criterion IDs, revision bookkeeping,
evidence rules, retry instructions, or review gates in the user prompt merely to
make the agent succeed. If the agent needs them, establish whether they belong in
plugin discovery/instructions, tool results, or server-enforced behavior. Asking
the user is appropriate for real ambiguity, not missing internal process guidance.

Keep two evaluation tracks and label results separately:

- **Mechanics tests:** detailed scripted or simulated exercises checking APIs,
  state invariants, and recovery. Useful diagnostics, not product-readiness proof.
- **User-realistic trials:** fresh conversations with ordinary outcome prompts,
  the installed plugin, and the same context available to a normal user. Check
  whether the agent discovers Blume, starts/joins correctly, maintains work,
  generates/runs tests, links evidence, and respects review boundaries without
  procedural coaching. Include corrections, ambiguous delivery association,
  resumed conversations, and prompts that should not activate Blume.

Keep the evaluator's expected sequence and assertions outside the tested agent's
context. Configure disposable environments and permission boundaries through the
harness, rather than embedding the answer in the prompt. Retain both the initial
prompt and all injected instructions/tool context so failures can be attributed
to the correct layer. Record any human/evaluator rescue as intervention; a coached
recovery must not count as an unassisted pass. Repeat with varied natural phrasing
and reserve unseen scenarios to avoid tuning solely to the benchmark prompts.

Architecture comparisons must eventually use this user-realistic track. A design
that succeeds only when the prompt tells it the entire Blume process has not
shown that its plugin configuration is sufficient.

### Stage model usage deliberately

Use Terra for economical early iteration and mechanical debugging. Its results
alone do not establish how the finished experience performs with stronger models.
Preserve this staged evaluation plan to control usage:

1. **Terra:** resolve major tool, runtime, discovery, and workflow defects first.
2. **GPT-5.6 Sol:** once a set of tests is further along and major defects are
   addressed, run a small, deliberately selected set of realistic user trials.
   Focus on representative end-to-end behavior and unresolved model-sensitive
   questions; do not repeat the entire exploratory matrix on the stronger model.
3. **GPT-6 Astra:** eventually run **one** carefully prepared realistic end-to-end
   trial when the app and plugin are ready for a meaningful final evaluation.

Before each stronger-model trial, confirm the environment works with inexpensive
checks, define what the trial should establish, and retain the exact model,
configuration, prompt, evidence, interventions, and usage. Do not use expensive
trials to rediscover known infrastructure failures. Fix those first. Do not launch
additional Astra trials automatically; further runs require a user decision.

Keep the same realistic-prompt standard across models. Report stronger-model
results separately from Terra results. One Astra success is valuable evidence,
not proof of universal reliability; avoid broad claims from this deliberately
small sample.

## Completion standard — proposed

Completion means a reproducible end-to-end journey with working user decisions,
real execution and evidence, durable state, and no known critical gaps. Passing
unit tests, a deployed service, or a polished fixture demonstration alone is
insufficient. State any remaining limitations explicitly; do not call an
unexercised path complete. Nothing here authorizes merging into main.

After approval, the hourly reviewer will challenge completion claims against
this document and request concrete proof or further work where gaps remain.
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/plugin-architecture-levers.md">
# Plugin architecture: available pieces

Research snapshot: 2026-09-25. Design inventory, not a claim of installed support.
Evaluate combinations against [the expected process](expected-delivery-process.md).

## Scope: Deliveries only

This inventory targets Deliveries in the Blume desktop app (`apps/desktop`; the former
standalone `apps/control-plane` shell is retired) and its Deliveries plugin/MCP. Keep
installations, endpoints, test accounts/projects, and proof records explicitly labeled by
channel.

## What "the plugin" means

"The Blume plugin" is everything the Blume installer puts into a harness, not only
what that harness's plugin or marketplace format can carry. Nothing needs to be
publishable on a harness marketplace. When a harness's plugin format cannot carry a
piece Blume needs (for example, hooks in Codex), the installer, run as a terminal
command or through a prompt to an agent, writes it directly into that harness's own
configuration. It still stays inside the harness home it was given (`CODEX_HOME` or
`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`), and it records what it wrote so `verify` and `uninstall` can
check and undo it.

**Plugin components** are the kinds of things the plugin can install:

- the MCP server and its tools;
- hooks;
- skills;
- rules and server instructions;
- scripts (the bridge);
- docs.

Choose components for what they can do in each harness, not for whether a
marketplace format supports them.

## 1. Getting the agent to use Blume

| Piece | Parameters to vary | Role and limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project instructions / rules | Global vs repository scope; always-loaded vs conditional; length; precedence | Establish default behavior and repo policy. A Markdown rules file is not automatically loaded by every harness. Instruction rules are distinct from executable permission rules. |
| Skills | Trigger description; one workflow vs focused skills; explicit vs inferred activation; progressive reference loading; scripts/examples | Teach when and how to use Blume without permanently loading the entire manual. Discovery is not guaranteed activation. |
| MCP server instructions | Short orientation; first-call guidance; recovery instructions | Orient clients that expose them to the model. Not a universal system prompt or guaranteed conversation-start trigger. |
| Lifecycle hooks | Startup/resume/compaction; prompt submission; before/after tools; stopping; matching; timeout; blocking vs context injection | Restore delivery context or check missing bookkeeping at specific events. Host-specific, needs installation/trust and coverage tests. Avoid an expensive inference call on every event. |
| Explicit entry point | Copyable setup prompt; terminal command; skill/slash command; connect/join prompt | Reliable user-initiated entry and fallback when automatic discovery is unsupported. |

Skills complement server actions with workflow guidance ([OpenAI skills](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/concepts/skills)).
Plugin packaging can combine skills, MCP and hooks, but installed hooks require
trust and executable scripts in the actual environment ([packaging](https://developers.openai.com/plugins/build/plugins)).
Codex documents startup, compaction and tool hooks, with coverage exceptions;
Claude has its own event/output contract. Neither should be treated as a universal
security boundary ([Codex hooks](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/hooks),
[Claude hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks)).

## 2. MCP capabilities

| Piece | Parameters to vary | Blume experiment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tools | Granularity/count; names/descriptions; typed arguments; required fields; enums; defaults; atomic vs separate operations | Compare granular task/evidence edits with intent-level operations such as begin attempt or submit for review. |
| Tool results | Structured output/schema; short text; resource links; images; actionable errors; state/version receipts | Return authoritative state, missing requirements and legal next actions, rather than an ambiguous success string or an enormous ledger. |
| Tool annotations | Read-only, destructive, idempotent and open-world hints | Help clients present actions. Hints do not enforce authorization or implement idempotency. |
| Resources/templates | URI-addressed context; revision-specific snapshots; task tree; acceptance coverage; pagination | Read delivery context on demand instead of requiring every fact to be another tool. A client decides whether/how resources enter model context. |
| Prompts | Named parameterized workflow templates and entry points | Offer start/join/review workflows. A listed prompt is not automatically injected into every conversation. |
| Argument completion | Completion of prompt/resource-template arguments | Help supported clients select delivery/repo identifiers; not general automatic filling of every tool argument. |
| Change notifications/subscriptions | Resource updates; catalog changes; reconnect handling | Surface new approvals/results. A notification is not a portable instruction to wake an idle agent. Retain a read/poll fallback. |
| Elicitation | Supported forms or URL flows; cancel/decline behavior | Ask for ambiguous delivery selection or configuration. Product approval still needs authenticated, revision-bound server validation. |
| Sampling | Request model work through a supporting client; model preferences; tool use where supported | Optional bounded analysis assistance. Not a guaranteed background model, and not access to the entire client conversation. |
| Roots | Client-provided workspace roots | Assist repository association; roots are not credentials or an enforced filesystem sandbox. |
| Long-running execution | Task extension support; job handles; status/results/cancel; progress | Keep browser tests observable and recoverable. MCP execution tasks are different from Blume's delivery task tree. |
| Transport/authentication | Local stdio bridge vs remote HTTP; capability/version discovery; connection identity; timeouts/retries | Compare setup friction and recovery, preserving scoped authorization and request cancellation. |
| Optional MCP UI | Supported UI extensions and resource presentation | Could assist setup, but does not replace the requested Electron review experience. Treat as client-specific, not baseline MCP behavior. |

Sources: [tools and results](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools),
[resources](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/resources),
[prompts, 2025 revision](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/server/prompts),
[elicitation](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/client/elicitation),
[sampling](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/client/sampling),
[protocol overview](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/basic),
[tasks extension draft](https://tasks.extensions.modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/draft/tasks).

### Version and compatibility gate

Do not mix protocol revisions. The 2026-07-28 specification changes cross-request
state and input requests; list endpoints must not vary per connection. Tasks also
have an extension path distinct from the earlier experimental feature. Therefore,
“state-aware tools” should initially mean stable tools returning valid next actions
and enforcing preconditions, not a catalog secretly changing after each call.
See [the revision changelog](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/changelog).

For each isolated harness record: executable/version, transport, supported protocol,
advertised capabilities, plugin manifest/version, hooks installed/trusted, and
whether each mechanism actually reaches the model or user. Probe discovery,
invocation, resume/compaction, cancellation and unsupported-feature fallbacks.
Mark each capability documented / advertised / experimentally verified separately.

## 3. Product mechanisms outside MCP

These are equally important pieces; MCP does not supply them automatically:

- **State machine:** phases that follow where the work is (any move is recorded with
  the steps it skipped, never refused), complete review coverage, revision-bound
  human approval as evidence rather than a gate, and explicit blocked states. Separate beginning an operation from
  proving its completion, so Merge and Deploy can describe work in progress.
- **Atomic operations:** bind attempt, revision and related task IDs together;
  publish immutable evidence; validate concurrency and retry keys on the server.
- **Context policy:** ask/default/repository rules, delivery matching, authoritative
  join handles and resumption. Never equate a transport connection with a delivery.
- **External integrations:** GitHub repository/PR/run association, workflow graph,
  deployment status and authenticated Electron decisions. Prefer observed events
  over agent self-reports where an authoritative integration exists.
- **Packaging and recovery:** self-contained installation, connection diagnostics,
  upgrades, revocation and safe restart. Documentation/scripts reduce setup work;
  they do not prove the right instructions were loaded.

## 4. Current implementation evidence

Read in MCP-owner checkout `4047` at this research snapshot:

- `controlMcp.ts` declares tools and server instructions for Deliveries; the hosted
  routes (`controlHostedLedger.ts`) serve them, and `controlPlaneCli.ts` starts the
  plugin's stdio bridge. Do not assume they expose every MCP primitive.
- `plugin.ts` version 0.5.5 generates a discoverable skill, rules, bridge/config
  and documentation; it explicitly says hooks are not installed.
- Separate `protocol.ts` implements resource/template and prompt handlers for
  another user-agent MCP surface. This belongs to a different surface and is reference only, not
  evidence those capabilities reach the current Deliveries client or a decision
  to share its implementation.
- Installed client support for the optional mechanisms above remains to be probed.
  The screenshot's tool count is not an architectural requirement.

## 5. Candidate combinations to test

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Native skill discovery] --> B[Model follows workflow]
  B --> C[Granular MCP tools]
  C --> D[Validated Blume state]
  D --> B
```

**A: Instructions plus granular tools.** Baseline: portable and flexible, but many
ordering/attribution decisions remain with the model.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Small entry skill] --> B[Join and read context]
  B --> C[Intent-level MCP operation]
  C --> D[Atomic state and evidence validation]
  D --> E[Receipt and allowed next actions]
  E --> C
```

**B: Workflow operations plus progressive context.** Move fragile multi-call
sequences into typed operations; measure whether abstraction hides useful control.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Start or resume hook] --> B[Repo policy and delivery context]
  B --> C[Skill and workflow tools]
  C --> D[Authoritative state]
  E[Post-tool or stop hook] --> F[Check missing checkpoint]
  F --> B
```

**C: Event-assisted workflow.** Add narrow hooks to B only where they improve
measured discovery/resumption/completeness. Test startup races, denied trust,
latency and repeated-stop loops. Keep hard state invariants in the server.

Hold scenarios/models/permissions constant initially. Change one layer at a time
before comparing full combinations. Use repeated real-agent trials and the expected
process as the behavioral scorecard; report violations, recovery, user effort,
latency and cost. No candidate is selected yet.
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/preview-development.md">
# Running Deliveries against a PR preview

Integration testing of hosted Deliveries happens only against a pull request's Product PR
Preview deployment set, controlled by pushing to that PR. Local, unpushed service changes
cannot be tested against hosted services.

1. Commit and push the exact change to a same-repository PR (draft is fine).
2. Wait for the **Product PR Preview** workflow for that head SHA to finish. It deploys the
   PR's Auth, the Deliveries runtime and its containers, runs the Deliveries smoke,
   and only then records the manifest.
3. From the same checkout, with `HEAD` equal to the PR head:

   ```sh
   export CLOUDFLARE_WORKERS_SUBDOMAIN=<account DNS label>
   pnpm dev
   ```

   The launcher prints `backend environment: PR #<n> · preview-pr-<n>-<sha>`. The main process
   receives `BLUME_AUTH_URL=https://blume-auth-pr-<n>.<account>.workers.dev` and
   `BLUME_CONTROL_REMOTE_ENDPOINT=https://blume-deliveries-runtime-pr-<n>.<account>.workers.dev`;
   the ledger worker forwards signed-in requests to that hosted runtime. There is no local
   ledger.

4. Sign in on the Blume account screen with **New here? Create an account**. Social
   providers are disabled in previews and production credentials never work there. Accounts,
   deliveries and evidence live in the PR's isolated D1, Durable Objects and R2 and are
   deleted when the PR closes. Cookies are stored per issuer, so switching between production
   and different PRs never reuses a session.

Failure messages name the missing prerequisite: no account label, no manifest for the exact
SHA (push or wait), a registry or runtime mismatch, or a conflicting preset `BLUME_AUTH_URL` /
`BLUME_CONTROL_REMOTE_ENDPOINT`. Without a PR preview, `BLUME_USE_PRODUCTION_BACKENDS=1` with
explicit HTTPS `BLUME_CONTROL_REMOTE_ENDPOINT` and `BLUME_AUTH_URL` is the only alternative.
Deployment details are in the
[Deliveries preview runbook](../../../../services/deliveries-runtime/docs/preview.md).
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/projects.md">
# Projects

A project is a named set of repositories. Deliveries belong to a project; agent setup belongs to a repository.

## Model

- **Every repository starts as its own project.** The ledger has no record for it. The project's id is the repository identity (`github.com/owner/name`, a `file:` path), and its name is the short repository label.
- **A record appears** once a person renames a project, merges projects or moves a repository, once an agent registers its project, or when a person sets one up (`ControlState.projects`). A repository is in at most one record.
- **People set projects up themselves.** Projects › Add project (`?add=1`) lists the repositories and folders in no project yet (this computer's checkouts and folders, then the GitHub repositories Blume can read) and creates a record from the chosen ones (`project_create`). A project's Sources card adds more the same way (`project_add_sources`). Both refuse a location that is already in a project: moving one between projects stays Move, which keeps its deliveries in view.
- **A delivery starts in one repository** (`Delivery.project`) and belongs to that repository's project. `Delivery.repositories` lists the other repositories it reached.
- **Setup stays per repository.** A project page lists its repositories, and each one opens the shared Setup view for that repository, read from its default branch on GitHub. There is no project-level setup.
- **Applications belong to projects.** An application is what runs and is tested (a website, a desktop app, an API) with its surfaces, environments and scenarios (`TestApplication`). Each one belongs to exactly one project (`TestApplication.project`: the record id, or the repository of a repository that is its own project) and takes its code location from it; a project can have several. Agents configure applications through `blume_setup` op update. MCP test execution is unavailable; existing applications and test history remain readable through `blume_tests` op get. A conversation without a project is asked to register one with `blume_project_register` first. Older ledgers, which made one application per delivery repository named after it, are attached to the owning project on read, one legacy application per project (`testApplications.ts`). When a project gets a record or merges, its applications follow.
- **Agents without a repository** (`unassigned`) never join a project.

The model lives in `packages/app/core/src/features/controlPlane/projects.ts` (`@blume/app-core/control-plane-projects`). It depends only on the runtime-neutral `@blume/projects-identity` (canonical repository matching), so the ledger, the renderer and the plugin bridge share it.

## What an agent sees

An agent's repository is the one its conversation reported. It can read and work on:

1. deliveries in its repository's project;
2. deliveries that reached its repository;
3. deliveries it already joined;
4. deliveries a message linked for it.

A delivery-linked message is the invitation to work across repositories. It can come from the person (the Agents page composer lists every delivery) or from an agent that can already see the delivery. `blume_context` returns the agent's `project`.

## Joining projects

When an agent works on a delivery from a repository in another project, the delivery reaches that repository:

- **The person invited the agent, and the other project is only that repository with no deliveries of its own:** it joins the delivery's project at once. This quietly covers the common first cross-repository delivery. An agent's invitation never joins projects: the reached repository sees that delivery, and the person is asked as below.
- **Otherwise:** the person is asked. The Projects page shows a suggestion on both projects. The person can merge the projects, move only that repository, or keep them separate. "Keep separate" is remembered for that pair of repositories.

Merges are not automatic beyond the lone-repository case, for three reasons:

- One shared library would otherwise snowball unrelated projects together.
- Agents on unrelated work would start seeing each other's deliveries without the person deciding.
- The person owns project boundaries.

A merge can be undone: "Make it its own project" splits a repository out again.

## Operations

These are human-only ledger operations:

- `project_create` creates a project, with its name, from repositories and folders in no project yet.
- `project_add_sources` adds repositories and folders in no project yet to a project.
- `project_rename` gives a project a name (and creates its record).
- `project_merge` moves every repository of one project into another.
- `project_move_repository` moves one repository into another project.
- `project_split_repository` makes a repository its own project again.
- `project_suggestion_dismiss` keeps two repositories in separate projects.

`project_create` and `project_add_sources` refuse a location that is already in a project, including a repository that is its own project with deliveries: moving one between projects stays `project_move_repository`.
</file>

<file path="docs/deliveries/ui-principles.md">
# Blume UI principles

A practical guide to the delivery app. Start with layout, then use the examples
for the component you are working on. How the product treats people's decisions
is in the [product principles](../../../../docs/product-principles.md); how the
code is built is in the
[engineering rules](../../../../docs/architecture-patterns.md#engineering-rules).

> **The common thread:** one clear destination, shared components, and evidence
> close to the decision it supports.

---

## 01 · Layout and navigation

There are **two fundamental page layouts: Columns and Custom**. Both live inside
the same app shell. Cards, tabs, and sub-pages are parts of those layouts, not
additional top-level layout types.

### The hierarchy

| Level | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| **App shell** | Top bar, app navigation, and the page bar with breadcrumbs and page actions |
| **Page layout** | Columns or Custom, filling the workspace below the page bar |
| **Regions and containers** | Lists, main content, Page Column Cards, and their tabs |
| **Sub-page** | A detail route opened within the workspace, using its own content layout |

**Read the screenshot from outside in:** app navigation at the far left, page bar
across the top, then the page’s list and main content below. The app navigation
is not the list column.

![App navigation, page bar, and the top of the delivery workspace](../../design-assets/ui-principles/layout-shell-hierarchy.png "Layout overview")

### Columns: list, content, supporting information

Use **ColumnLayout** when selecting an item changes the main content and related
information belongs beside it. Deliveries in List view, Tests, and Agents use this
pattern. Regions are optional; a page does not need all three.

![Columns layout with delivery list, main explanation, and Getting started card](../../design-assets/ui-principles/layout-columns-overview.png "Layout overview")

| Region, left to right | Purpose | Example above |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary column** | Choose what to open | Deliveries list |
| **Main content** | Read or work on the selected destination | Delivery explanation; delivery details after selection |
| **Supporting column** | Related information or actions | Getting started; tasks and other supporting views after selection |

The primary column meets the page edges. The supporting column usually contains a
**Page Column Card** with an inset, shared header, and optional tabs or footer.
A Page Column Card is a container inside a region, not another page layout.

![A Page Column Card header with Tasks, PRs, Tests, and Agents tabs](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-tabs-counts.png)


### Column spacing and resize boundaries

Use one **24px content gutter** on each side of the main content. The gap from
content to a supporting Page Column Card must match the gap from the primary
column to content. Do not add a second inset on the card’s content-facing edge.
The card keeps its **12px outer inset** at the top, bottom, and window-facing side.

The resize hit area sits **on the card edge**, never in the middle of the gap:
the left edge of a right-hand card, or the right edge of a left-hand card.
Sub-page overlays retain their own **12px inset** beside an uncovered supporting
card. The 24px main-content gutter rule does not remove this card-to-card gap.

Keep the generous invisible pointer target and keyboard resizing. Sidecar pages
keep their existing full-width layout, without expanded-mode gutters or handles.

### Custom: a workspace with its own arrangement

Use **CustomLayout** when the content needs a different spatial arrangement, such
as the delivery kanban board. It fills the same workspace beneath the page bar,
without imposing list, content, and supporting regions.

![Custom layout showing the delivery board arranged by phase](../../design-assets/ui-principles/layout-custom-board.png "Layout overview")

A board lane is part of the board, not a Page Column. Keep horizontal scrolling
for the board. Custom means freedom to arrange the workspace, not different
headers, badges, surfaces, or navigation rules.

### Sub-pages: details within either layout

Both Columns and Custom can open a **SubPageLayout**. In expanded mode it is an
inset card over the regions it covers. Uncovered regions remain usable. A task
may cover only the content; verification or a test run can cover the full workspace.
The covered area uses a flat backdrop.

A sub-page can itself use Columns. In this test-run example, the sub-page header
sits above a scenario list, selected evidence, and a supporting Linked tasks card.

![Test-run sub-page header above its scenario, evidence, and linked-task regions](../../design-assets/ui-principles/layout-expanded-regions.png "Layout overview")

The **sub-page header identifies the route**; a **card header labels a container**
inside it. A screenshot gallery is a dialog, not a sub-page.
See [Back, close, and motion](#07-back-close-and-motion) for return behavior.

### Sidecar: the same hierarchy, one destination at a time

When there is not enough room for useful columns, show **pages and tabs** instead
of stacking the list, selected details, and supporting column vertically.
Use the product container width to decide, not the surrounding browser width.

| Expanded region | Compact presentation |
| --- | --- |
| Primary list and selected content | List page, then detail page with Back |
| Main content and tabbed supporting card | Overview first, then the supporting tabs |
| Main content and an untabbed supporting card | Overview and one named supporting tab |
| Inset sub-page card | Full-page detail with the regular main-content background |

**Tabbed supporting card:** a delivery becomes Overview, Tasks, PRs, Tests, and
Agents. Keep the selected tab when returning.

![Sidecar delivery tabs with Overview before Tasks, PRs, Tests, and Agents](../../design-assets/ui-principles/sidecar-tabs.png)

**Untabbed supporting card:** Overview and Linked tasks become two tabs. The Back
action remains separate from those choices.

![Sidecar Overview and Linked tasks tabs](../../design-assets/ui-principles/layout-sidecar-two-tabs.png)

**Full-page details:** use internal padding without an outer card gutter, dark
backdrop, or outer shadow. The content reaches the page edges.

![Task details on the regular full-width sidecar surface](../../design-assets/ui-principles/sidecar-page-surface.png)

<details>
<summary>Avoid: carrying the expanded card backdrop into sidecar</summary>

This dark strip and inset card are inappropriate in compact mode.

![Rejected dark gutter outside a compact task page](../../design-assets/ui-principles/sidecar-gutter-detail.png)

</details>

### Resizing preserves the place you are in

- Keep selection, active tabs, filters, and scroll positions.
- Resizing and switching tabs do not add navigation history.
- Expand the native window in width only, on its current display. Preserve height
  and vertical position; use smooth easing and respect reduced motion.
- Only sections of the same destination may stack. Independent regions become
  pages or tabs. Custom boards retain their own horizontal arrangement.

These are interaction requirements. The screenshots above show the resulting
layouts; they do not verify motion or navigation history.

---

## 02 · Headers and typography

**SN Pro regular (400)** is the body default; use heavier SN Pro for emphasis.
**Gelica medium (500)** is for content headings. Keep badge icons in regular strokes.

- Use the shared card header: SN Pro, a small concept/status icon, one-line
  truncated title, consistent height/padding, and a subtle bottom divider.
- Current typography experiment: uppercase container titles and tab labels with
  subtle letter spacing. Content headings and header action labels keep their usual case.
- `CardHeader` owns the title/tabs header surface and optional Back/Close controls.
  `CardHeaderTabsList` uses its tabs mode and retains the shared keyboard/tab behavior.
  A panel has **either a title header or a tab header, never both**.
  `PageColumnCard` enforces that choice through its props. A separately divided
  footer panel can have its own title, such as Revision approval.
- Sub-page layouts supply navigation callbacks and focus refs to `CardHeader`;
  the header does not invent navigation history. Back, Escape, and Close retain
  the existing route and compact-mode behavior.
- Section headers such as **How to use Blume** and **Linked tasks** use SN Pro
  semibold (600) for the full label.
- Entity headers emphasize only the type prefix: **Task:** Persist basket changes.
  Use semibold (600) for “Task:” / “Test run:” and regular (400) for the entity name.
- Tab labels use semibold (600) when selected and regular (400) otherwise.
  Counts and secondary metadata stay regular and visually quieter; header actions
  retain the shared Button styling. Do not use bold (700) as the default header weight.
- Optional counts and actions align at the trailing edge. Task headers use TaskIcon.
- Page Column Cards, regular titled cards, and sub-page cards share this treatment.
  Tabbed headers share its height and divider. Gelica belongs to content/page headings,
  not container labels. Phase identity continues to use DeliveryPhaseBadge.

### Section header

the entire “How to use Blume” label is semibold; the icon stays small.


![How to use Blume card header with a small icon and semibold SN Pro label](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-section-header.png)

### Entity header

“Task:” is semibold, while the task name stays regular.

![Task header with semibold type prefix and regular entity name](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-entity-header.png)

  and floating Page Column Cards use their existing contextual surface/elevation rules.

## 04 · Status, tasks, and lists

Reuse the same components wherever the same information appears. Color supports
labels and icons; it never carries status on its own.

### Two separate signals

Passed describes the test result; Needs review or Reviewed
describes the human decision. Use a tinted result badge and a linen neutral review
badge, with different icon colors for the review states.

![Passed result alongside Needs review](../../design-assets/ui-principles/result-review-badges.png)

![Passed result alongside Reviewed](../../design-assets/ui-principles/reviewed-result-badges.png)

### Task identity

a quiet number badge sits beside the status on a task page.
The number supplements the task icon; it does not replace it in breadcrumbs.

![Subtle task number beside its status](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-task-number-status.png)

### Task tree

indentation conveys ancestry, number badges align at the trailing
edge, and the phase belongs to the root. A half-circle means in progress, a filled
check means completed, and an open circle means not started.

![Root task with an in-progress icon, completed and open children, and trailing task numbers](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-task-states-tree.png)

### Breadcrumb identity

use the task status icon with its name, rather than the
number badge. Truncate long labels without displacing the icon.

![Task breadcrumb with status icons and truncated task name](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-breadcrumb-task-icons.png)

### Phase identity

use the shared phase badge, including its icon, color, border,
and label; a phase card does not invent its own treatment.

In a delivery's page header the phase badge is also a menu button
(`DeliveryPhaseBadge` with `menu`, rendered by the shared `EntityMenuButton`): it keeps
the badge's icon, color, border and label, adds a small caret, and opens the eight
phases with the current one checked. Choosing another sets the delivery there
(`delivery_phase_set`), forward or back, through the same action path and error
display as the page's other person operations. The visit it opens says "Moved here
by you" with the steps the move skipped. Badges elsewhere (rows, tiles, timelines)
stay plain labels.

The official phase palette comes from [Delivery lifecycle PR #539](https://github.com/blumepage/sidecar-prototype/pull/539).
`theme.css` owns the exact `--phase-*` values; graph lines, icons, progress segments,
and timeline dots use these colors. Badge text and opaque surfaces use matching
light/dark ramps for readability. Phase colors remain independent of the selected flower theme.

| Phase | Color | Canonical OKLCH |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start | Slate | `68% 0.025 255` |
| Learn | Blue | `60% 0.15 250` |
| Plan | Violet | `58% 0.17 285` |
| Build | Magenta | `58% 0.18 320` |
| Test | Rose | `60% 0.2 355` |
| Review | Coral | `63% 0.19 30` |
| Ready | Amber | `72% 0.15 65` |
| Merge | Green | `62% 0.15 135` |
| Deploy | Teal | `59% 0.15 165` |
| Live | Cyan-blue | `50% 0.14 225` |

![Shared phase badge with icon and phase color](../../design-assets/ui-principles/components-phase-badge.png)

small gaps and rounded ends distinguish the segments. Keep the label
and completion count together above the bar.

## 07 · Back, close, and motion

> **Review pending:** the expanded behavior is approved. Sidecar Back, Escape, and close still need interaction review.

- Preserve the existing expanded-mode behavior; the user has approved it.
- Back returns to the actual preceding destination and names it concisely, without
  a “Back to” prefix. Truncate long destination names. Inferred breadcrumb ancestors
  are not necessarily navigation history.
- In expanded mode, X closes the current sub-page card to its underlying page.
  Escape follows the existing history-aware behavior; dialogs/popovers consume it first.
- In sidecar/mobile, render details as pages, not floating cards. Use one clear Back
  action. Avoid duplicate Back bars or showing both Back and X for the same operation.
- In sidecar, Back and Escape return from supporting details to the scenario, then
  to the scenario list, then to the originating page. Nested task/test pages retrace
  visited pages. Tabs retain their selection when returning; changing a tab does not
  add history. Dialogs consume Escape first. Resize never changes this history.
- Sidecar Escape/X/Back behavior is not yet approved: finish and review it before
  writing the full documentation.

### Expanded close

X belongs at the trailing edge of the sub-page header and returns
to the underlying page. This crop shows its placement, not an Escape history test.

![Close button at the trailing edge of the expanded sub-page header](../../design-assets/ui-principles/navigation-expanded-close.png)

### Sidecar return

a concise destination label accompanies the Back arrow. It names
the preceding destination; it is not a second title or a duplicate close action.

![Sidecar Back arrow labeled Scenarios](../../design-assets/ui-principles/navigation-sidecar-back.png)

### Disclosures

a quiet chevron and label reveal supporting detail. Animate opening
and closing with the same motion treatment; keep the trigger keyboard-accessible.

![Technical details disclosure in its closed state](../../design-assets/ui-principles/navigation-disclosure-closed.png)

![Technical details disclosure expanded to show supporting step notes](../../design-assets/ui-principles/navigation-disclosure-open.png)

The closed/open pair illustrates disclosure structure. Timing, easing, reduced motion,
native window resizing, and actual Back/Escape history still need interaction review;
static screenshots are not acceptance evidence for those behaviors.

---

## 08 · Before you ship

- Reuse shared primitives and run design lint.
- Check expanded and sidecar layouts for overflow and readable spacing.
- Follow Back and Escape through nested pages and dialogs.
- Check transitions, keyboard focus, and reduced motion.
- Test native window resizing in Electron.

Static screenshots illustrate appearance. They do not prove interaction behavior.
